Clarity.justification: The paper is well-structured with clear sections (Abstract, Introduction, Related Work, Method, Experiments, Results, Discussion). Contributions are explicitly listed. Methods describe loss-based detection, linear probes, and implementation details. Results include quantitative tables and figures matching the claims (e.g., 8.3× loss ratio, 10.7 pp probe gap). Minor issues include occasional hand-wavy phrasing around base-rate bounds, but overall logical and coherent.

Novelty.justification: Builds directly on JTT, SPARE, and LA-SSL by shifting from fixed thresholds or aggregate speed to per-sample loss trajectories. Provides a refinement of simplicity-bias theory under transfer learning (magnitude gap vs. temporal gap). Incremental rather than groundbreaking; no new datasets, architectures, or end-to-end robustness algorithm.

Soundness.justification: Experimental design uses standard Waterbirds + pretrained ResNet-18; loss separation is statistically significant (Mann-Whitney p < 10^{-14}). Linear-probe results confirm the claimed mechanism and match the provided figures. Code logs show consistent training and probing runs. Limitations are acknowledged (single dataset, no intervention test, pretrained-only). One minor inconsistency: both probes peak at epoch 81, which is explained but deviates from classic simplicity-bias timing predictions.

Significance.justification: Addresses a practical robustness problem and demonstrates a usable early-training signal for minority detection. Precision (32.9 %) is near the theoretical base-rate ceiling, suggesting the signal is strong. However, downstream utility (e.g., improved worst-group accuracy via loss-based reweighting) is not evaluated, limiting immediate impact.

strengths: Clear statistical demonstration of loss separation and mechanistic verification via probes
Explicit characterization of precision limits under class imbalance
weaknesses: Single-dataset evaluation and absence of any intervention experiment
No demonstration that the detected samples improve worst-group accuracy when used for reweighting
